title: You Have to Let Go: Promote Into a Mating Net
summary: Use promotion to overload the rook: accepting the queen permits pawn mate, while declining still leaves a forcing attack.

nodes.question: Why promote when the rook can take the queen?
nodes.explanation: Kf6 controls g5, g6 and g7. After d8=Q, the rook can capture on d8, but abandoning the fifth rank permits g5 mate. Other defenses need checking too; the saved finite strategy covers all nineteen Black replies.

branches.title: Source line: accept the queen, allow pawn mate
commentary: Begin after Kf6 and Rd5. The rook appears to stop promotion, but the white king supports the g-pawn and seals the opposing king’s escape squares.
d8=Q makes a queen and offers it to the rook. Promotion does not check Kh6; Black has nineteen legal replies, including checks and hxg4.
Rxd8 takes the queen but removes the rook from the fifth rank. The rook can no longer take a pawn on g5.
g5# checks h6 with the pawn. Kf6 protects g5 and covers g6/g7, while Black’s own h5/h7 pawns occupy the remaining flights. This is actual checkmate with every queenside pawn retained.
branches.explanation: g5# checks h6 with the pawn. Kf6 protects g5 and covers g6/g7, while Black’s own h5/h7 pawns occupy the remaining flights. This is actual checkmate with every queenside pawn retained.

branches.title: Independent defense: keep the rook on g5
commentary: Compare the rook defense that prevents an immediate g5 pawn move. This representative continuation is independent analysis, not a recovered source variation.
d8=Q keeps the protected king on f6 as the anchor of the mating net.
Rg5 occupies the pawn’s target and blocks its advance, but lets the queen attack along the f8–h6 diagonal.
Qf8+ checks diagonally. Kf6 controls g6 and g7, while h5 and h7 remain occupied by Black’s pawns.
Rg7 is the only legal reply, interposing on the queen’s diagonal to h6. The rook has merely changed which mating threat it must meet.
Qxg7# removes that interposer with check. Kf6 protects the queen on g7; the same king-and-pawn cage leaves no escape.

branches.explanation: Qxg7# removes that interposer with check. Kf6 protects the queen on g7; the same king-and-pawn cage leaves no escape.

branches.title: Independent defense: a waiting pawn move loses at once
commentary: Compare a legal waiting move instead of capturing the queen or meeting the mating attack. All four queenside pawns remain on their actual squares until moved.
d8=Q threatens more than the g-pawn advance: the queen can also reach the mating diagonal.
b5 advances the pawn from b7 two squares legally, but does not create an escape for Kh6 or interpose on f8–g7–h6.
Qf8# checks along that diagonal. Rd5 cannot interpose on g7 in one move, and Black’s king is boxed by Kf6 and its own h-pawns.

exercises.prompt: What makes accepting the queen fatal?
exercises.answer: Rxd8 abandons the fifth rank. The protected g-pawn advances to g5 with mate, and the rook cannot return to capture it.

exercises.prompt: Does the source rook capture prove the whole position by itself?
exercises.answer: No. Black has nineteen legal replies after promotion. A separate finite certificate checks every defense, including rook checks, Rg5 and hxg4, until actual mate.
